title: Research papers can now become AI agents that answer questions
key_facts: Paper2Agent, built by Stanford's Jiacheng Miao, James Zou and colleagues, turns a research paper and its shared code into an AI agent that answers questions by running the paper's own code.
Works through three agents that set up the software, turn methods into tools and test them; packaged with the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
26 of 100 biology papers could not be converted; 74 became working agents, 593 of 599 proposed tools passed tests.
On 300 questions the agents scored 91.2%, versus 80.3% for Claude working directly from the code.
AlphaGenome agent: 22 tools in about 45 minutes, $14, on a laptop.
Three linked agents helped point to GPR137 as a likely psoriasis gene using data earlier teams had collected; no new lab work.
Authors say researchers remain responsible for selecting directions and evaluating evidence.
quote_evidence: It works best on papers that come with usable code, and 26 of the 100 biology papers the team tried couldn't be converted.
No new lab work was done, since every check used data the earlier teams had already collected.
In every test here, the researchers chose which papers to connect.
why_it_matters_hint: Turning papers into tools could make published methods easier for other scientists to use.
notes: Journal or preprint venue not named in the article; findings are the authors' own tests. Kept at 5.
